title: ARC-001: Ultrasonic vs. Time-of-Flight Sensor Characterization
summary: I designed and ran a servo-swept test rig to measure exactly how an ultrasonic sensor and a time-of-flight sensor differ when they look at the same scene.
result: Compared two rangefinders against a six-object ground-truth scene and measured a 4.0× difference in angular resolution across 9,720 logged readings.
role: Personal project: fixture design, firmware, test plan, data analysis
spec: My first scanner (ARC-000) drew objects much wider than they were. I wanted to know why, and by how much, before choosing a sensor for future projects.

A printed fixture holds both sensors on one servo so every sample is a paired measurement of the same scene. I measured six objects into coordinates and used a Python ray-cast model to generate the true range at every scan angle.
20 sweeps, a 14-station range ladder from 100 to 750 mm, a 13-gap resolution ladder at 300 mm, and 200-sample static holds.
The time-of-flight sensor resolved two targets at 13.7° and the ultrasonic sensor needed 54.6°, a 4.0× difference.
Arduino (C++), Python, MATLAB, HC-SR04, VL53L1X, MG90S servo, I2C, SolidWorks, Bambu FDM
cover_alt: 3D-printed fixture holding a VL53L1X time-of-flight board above an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor, mounted on a servo at the edge of a table marked with hand-drawn angle lines.
cover_caption: The coaxial fixture. The time-of-flight sensor sits directly above the ultrasonic transducers so both sensors see the same scene at the same moment.
